utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, you maybe seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers with the Office of the Prosecutor. With me is co-counsel Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink is our case manager for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How is Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben is still ill at this point and he hopes to return to the office on Thursday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. We are assisted by our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic and good morning to you and your team. So a few housekeeping matters. Now, tomorrow, Wednesday, we will be sitting in Courtroom II, all right? And the day after, Thursday, we will be sitting in Courtroom III. The time is as today, 9.00 in the morning, but that's something that I wanted to alert you to. Second, there is -- we have received a copy of the Defence motion for the admission of the witness statement of Avdo Huseinovic, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. I suppose you know about it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having heard what Mr. Wubben had stated some time back, I take it that you are going to oppose this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are studying it and we will probably intend to have some opposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. When will we have the response?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we anticipate to file that early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we are not going to shorten the time limit, but please try to file it early next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. This covers that. This covers this. And this covers that. This is superseded by the other one. Any preliminaries on your part? MR. DI FAZIO: Just one matter regards the mechanics of this morning. Firstly, I apologise if I jump around from topic to topic in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not unusual. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not unusual, and perhaps forced a little by circumstances. Secondly, you've been very generous in allowing us changing the times. Should it -- for the morning breaks -- should I get to a point this morning where I need to confer with other members of the team and where shortly before a break I might ask for a somewhat early adjournment to enable me to do that. But other than that I expect things to do smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That wouldn't be any problems at all with that, Mr. Di Fazio. Any other preliminaries from the Defence? Nothing?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's bring the witness in and we take it up from where we left it yesterday. For the record, we are today once more sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis(A). And the reason being the same as it was yesterday, namely a legitimate impediment being an urgent personal reason of Judge Eser and the decision is taken because the remaining two judges, Judge Brydensholt and myself are satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to continue sitting without Judge Eser being present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to start with the cross-examination and hope we will be able to finish with you today and send you home. So, please, make yourself comfortable. May I remind you that you are still testifying under oath in terms of the solemn declaration rather that you made yesterday, and please try to answer all the questions that are put to you as briefly as possible, in a truthful manner and to the best of your ability. Okay. Thank you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, my name is Di Fazio. I have a few questions for you on behalf of the Prosecution. Do you know Mr. Oric, Mr. Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Naser Oric following the demilitarisation of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of him prior to the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under what circumstances did you meet him following demilitarisation? How did you come to meet him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not actually meet him. I did not know him from before. But when I went down to Srebrenica, I saw that it was him on the basis of what people were saying. But I did not get in touch with him in any way, and I do know that Mr. Naser had not even known about me until yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, sure. Okay. So it's clear that you heard about him through others?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your friends and acquaintances in Srebrenica? That's from whom you heard about him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard it from the people present, the people I talked to, and in their stories they used to mention that he was a good fighter but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So you heard his name mentioned by many people in Srebrenica when you went there following demilitarisation and always in the context of his being a good fighter?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard those stories from some of my friends but I did not actually meet him in person. So I'm not able to make any more extensive comments. I've told you that it was the first time I set eyes on him but I was not in any contact with him and I never talked to him myself. So what I knew is what I've told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. By the time demilitarisation came about, there had been a lot of fighting between Bosniak or -- the people besieged in the Srebrenica area and the Serbs, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't actually go along with the statement that there had been a lot of fighting. There was a lot of chasing of the Muslim population away from some locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really familiar with the idea of a direct battles being waged between the Serbs and the Muslims because in that case we would have had to have brigade and corps in order to be able to engage in battle with the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it another way, would you agree that in the time up to demilitarisation in March of 1993, the Muslim people in the Srebrenica area had shown a heroic resistance to Serb forces? Would you agree with that proposition, at least?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I did say that in my area, where I myself lived in the area of Poznanovici I said that in the beginning of the war and during the summer, we were surrounded and I know exactly what went on in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But anything else -- well, I can only conclude that the situation is much the same in other places. We were fighting for survival basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. You were fighting for survival and there would be a lot of people involved in that fighting for survival in the period of time leading up to demilitarisation of 1993, correct? A lot of men.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather disagree. There were quite a few homeless and the refugees as well who were fighting for their survival because they had been turned away from their homes and villages so the only way they could survive was to go back to those villages and look for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about starvation. I'm not asking you about the bad conditions in Srebrenica. I'm not asking you about the homeless people. I'm not asking you anything about those things. It's a very, very simple question. Up until the point of demilitarisation, there had been many people who had been fighting, men who had been fighting, to resist the Serb forces, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be good if the Prosecutor could specify what area he means because he's confusing the witness. The witness has replied that he know that is they were surrounded and he knows what happened in that particular area, and so he might be confused now. It would be better to specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is room for confusion. To me it has been clear throughout that we are talking about the Srebrenica area. So the witness, please, restrict his answer to the Srebrenica area. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was up until the point of demilitarisation, there had been many people who had been fighting, men who had been fighting the Serbs, resisting the Serbs, you would have to agree with that, surely. It's a very simple proposition.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've talked -- well, yesterday I remember I said that in Poznanovici we were surrounded and that there was a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget Poznanovici, Mr. Ramic, have you never heard about resistance in Srebrenica and its environs. It's also being put to you not only having heard of resistance in Srebrenica but heroic resistance in and around Srebrenica. Have you never heard of heroic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. resistance in and around Srebrenica during the relevant time, that is up to demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, later on I heard that there were those groups that offered resistance to the Serb forces but I disagree with the point being made by the Prosecution, Your Honour, in that there were supposed to be very many people offering resistance. There were many people but they had no weapons. We did not have any structures, brigades, corps, whatever. If only we had that we wouldn't have had the experience we had to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you've given me the impression that you have moved from absolute ignorance the events in Srebrenica because you were sort of cut off and restricted to your area only, to knowing also that there weren't that many resistance people involved in resistance and also that they were mostly unarmed. Now, please decide what you know and what you don't. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me approach it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness clarified he found that out later. Firstly, he's talking about what he knew in Poznanovici, then he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, this is not what he found out later. This is -- well, I mean I've been --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, he says, "Well, later on I heard that there were those groups that offered resistance." So he's clarified that later on he did learn. Your Honour is showing an animosity towards our witness which is not called for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm showing that he suddenly moved from absolute ignorance to knowing a little bit more than I thought he knew. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps I can make the job a little easier for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's say there weren't many resistance fighters. Let's say there was only a few. You'd have to agree that there was a heroic resistance by a few fighters, just a few. Would you agree with that proposition, at least?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There seems to be a misunderstanding here. I did say that I found out certain things after demilitarisation and there were some fighters, of course. It is only logical. Of course there were those groups. As we had a group in my village, Poznanovici - we got organised amongst ourselves - so in many other places there were similar groups which got organised in order to defend the defenceless people. So it can't be ruled out. And I simply can't agree with the fact that it was all well-organised and that there were very many people who were able to offer resistance in that way. That's what I disagree with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your position that there was no organised resistance is abundantly clear, okay. I understand that so please don't fret about my understanding then. My -- the point that I want to make is this: That there were quite a large number -- there were numbers of fighters who were resisting the Serbs, yet you, who didn't know Mr. Oric, heard about him in the context of being one of the -- a good fighter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether it was correct or not, I did tell you that I did not know him in person. But I did hear that story, yes. I can't confirm the truth of the story because I did not know him but I heard that story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've never met him, have you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Did the stories that you heard in Srebrenica following demilitarisation simply say that he was a good fighter? Or did they refer to him in any other capacity. For example, being a good leader? A good commander?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did not know him, so I was never in any contact with him. So I heard those stories according to which he was a good fighter and once again I can't confirm it and I did not hear any thing else really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other good fighters did you hear about following demilitarisation? Can you give us some names?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really remember about any other good fighters at the moment, Your Honour, because it is -- well it was a long time ago and so I can really remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were asked some questions about a place called Bajramovici. You recall those questions asked by Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me? I apologise for this paper shuffling. And you said yesterday that you weren't informed of the meeting at Bajramovici. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you in fact went further than that, not only that you hadn't heard of it but that it wouldn't have occurred. You were asked by Madam Vidovic this question and you gave this answer: "Were any of you present" -- question: "Were any of you present at this meeting? Did you ever hear about it?" I'm just quoting from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him quote. Provided you quote -- MR. DI FAZIO: This is the transcript I've got. Question: "Were any of you present at this meeting? Did you ever hear about it?" Answer: "No, nobody attended it. We would or I would have known about it." So, would you agree with me that your position on any meeting at Bajramovici is this: That certainly you never heard about it but more than that, it couldn't have happened because otherwise you would have known about it. Now, that's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question, Madam Vidovic. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you remember your answer, don't you, "no, nobody attended it, we would have -- we would or I would have known about it." You remember that, your answer, more importantly?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I see Madam Vidovic, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I want him to answer your question first, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I think he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think he has. He just keeps repeating that he remembers his question and answer yesterday. But hasn't answered your question. Your question was -- MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that in terms -- according to what you said yesterday, would you agree with me that your position on any meeting at Bajramovici is this: That certainly you never heard about it but more than that, it couldn't have happened because otherwise you would have known about it. MR. DI FAZIO: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that your position? If I'm not clear I will repeat the question. I will repeat the question. No, I want him to answer first, Madam Vidovic, because I think he can answer the question without any problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question? Your Honour, could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bear with me a little bit. So let's go further up again because this disappears. Now, Mr. Di Fazio reminded you that yesterday during the examination-in-chief, you were asked by Madam Vidovic the following question: You were reminded about the meeting supposedly that took place in Bajramovici. And you were asked by Madam Vidovic, "Were any of you present at this meeting? Did you ever hear about it?" And then, according to the transcript that you have, you answered, "No, nobody attended it. We would or I would have known about it." Now, Mr. Di Fazio wants you to explain whether or if in giving this answer you are stating that according to you, this meeting in Bajramovici never took place because if it had taken place, you would have known about it beforehand. Or you would have heard about it. MR. DI FAZIO: Or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or even afterwards, yeah. It's a very clear question, I mean, and I think you can answer it. This is why I told Madam Vidovic not to stand up because -- so that we can have an explanation from you without any prompting from the Defence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to explain. As to whether the meeting was held or not, I cannot know that 100 per cent, but I know that we did not attend, that nobody attended and that we would have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your answer therefore is that the fact that you did not know about it, the fact that no one of your group attended, it does not necessarily, does not necessarily follow that the meeting in Bajramovici to which you were referred to yesterday did not actually take place. This is your position, in other words? It's a syllogistic process, basically. I mean, it's pure syllogism. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps I can ask the witness this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to. I think -- his answer -- I mean, I think it is satisfactory, there is a satisfactory explanation. This is how it is. He confirms that he didn't know about it. He confirmed that no one attended it from his group, obviously because they had not been alerted or given notice of it, but at the same time he's not saying that therefore it follows that it never took place. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in that case I can move on to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I do recognise that it was important to clear up, but I think it has been cleared up. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, there is just one more matter that I want to raise about the matter, about the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your position now is that there could have been a meeting at Bajramovici but you certainly didn't know about it and your grouping, the people in your area, certainly didn't know about it. Would you agree with that? That's now your position, correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know about it, and as to whether it was held or not, I really cannot agree. All I know is that we didn't know whether the meeting was held or not or whether I agree or don't agree. It's not something that I can agree about or not agree about. I don't know if the meeting was held --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or not. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this up because it may or may not have a bearing, but -- and I may have -- he may have stated it yesterday and I would have missed it. Your village - let's restrict ourselves to Poznanovici - formed part of which commune?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ratkovici local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ratkovici formed part of which province? Or I'm calling it province. It could be county or I don't know because -- MR. DI FAZIO: Municipality, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Municipality, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of Srebrenica. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this. You have to acknowledge, both you and the Defence, that assuming -- because of course I'm not at this stage I definitely we definitely cannot attach to exhibit P73 a definitive credibility. So it's always subject to the probative value that we will eventually give to this document but the thing is that it's restricted to the area of Potocari, the town of Srebrenica itself, the area of Suceska, in Bajramovici, Bojna, Suceska again, and Skelani. And there were many other areas in the municipality of Srebrenica that could have been included and do not figure in. So -- all right? Do keep that in mind. So I'm not surprised at all even though the witness says that he would have known about it, I am -- given the circumstances in which they were living at the time I'm not surprised at all that he wasn't. MR. DI FAZIO: With respect, I'm not surprised either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not suggesting that we should be. That's not my point. I think -- just permit me to ask one more question on the topic. Perhaps my point might also emerge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, though, yesterday when you were answering questions from Madam Vidovic, your answer wasn't, Look I just don't know about any meeting at Bajramovici, it might have happened, I don't know if it happened or not. Your answer was very clear: Nobody attended it. I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think Your Honour that's why it was so important to clarify what the witness did say, and to then suggest now that he said something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I stopped. He's not saying anything different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may, just to be crystal clear, Your Honour. The question was: "Were you informed about the meeting in Bajramovici." "No." "Were any of you present? You, your group in Poznanovici present? Did you ever hear about it?" "No, nobody attended it." Now, "nobody," he's being asked about his group. "None of our group attended it otherwise I would have known about it." So to suggest he's saying something different, he's telling a terrible lie --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not saying anything different, and that's why I stopped Madam Vidovic from intervening because I knew why Mr. Di Fazio was putting the question and it was a very legitimate question. I would have put it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but now it's clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's clarified enough. I think I would move to something else Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy to do that, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear, absolutely. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked questions yesterday about P -- Exhibit P73, which relates to this meeting at Bajramovici and, now I know you don't know anything about it, but you were asked about the content of the document and in particular you were asked about a fellow called Ahmo Tihic, and essentially your evidence was that the -- the document is wrong in one respect at least, because it describes this fellow Tihic as an activist and an organiser in armed -- outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Skelani, and you say -- you said yesterday that's quite wrong he wasn't known at all. Would you -- do you recall that evidence, the effect of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't really say he wasn't known at all because the fact that he was in a position to give you answers -- not give you, give Madam Vidovic answers on Ahmo Tihic shows that he knew enough about him to be able to give the answers that he gave. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Well, I'll quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you want, you're free to rephrase your question. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll rephrase it, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What he contested to this document is the alleged or pretended role of an outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Skelani on the basis that in the area of Skelani there was no resistance at all. There was no leadership role assumed by Ahmo Tihic and the Muslim population just flew. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Escaped. That's what I understood yesterday and part of it was an answer to my question, too. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you just hear what His Honour had to say and do you now recall your evidence regarding Mr. Tihic from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I meant. He didn't put up resistance and he was not an organiser of the resistance in the villages in Skelani, because they were cleansed. Whether he led a group later or not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can answer this question now. If he was not an organiser, if there was no armed resistance, why would you -- I think -- Madam Usher, please, it's only fair that he's given -- he's shown P73 again. Why would we have stated in this document -- why would he -- we have his name in the first place, out of all the people in the Skelani area? Why him and not someone else? And secondly, why would he be described as an outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Skelani when according to you, and I have no reason to doubt your word, there was no resistance there and he was not an outstanding activist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that he wasn't an organiser of the resistance. As to what is here on paper, I'm not sure who drafted this paper. It's possible that in late August, a group was formed and perhaps Ahmo Tihic was a leader of that group and that's why there was stated. But about -- as for the period I was talking about in April, it's not true that he was one of the organisers, the villages wouldn't have gone without resistance. This is what I was explaining yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What group was it possible -- was possibly formed in late August?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late August -- I didn't say he wasn't a leader of any group, that he formed a group of Muslims and led the group. This is indisputable. But at the time, I really don't know -- I didn't know what this group was. Later, when I came to Srebrenica, I found out that he had formed a group and he was a leader of a group in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Look, I want to show you -- I'll withdraw that question. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction for the transcript. He said that he found out in Srebrenica that Ahmo Tihic had a group but not that Tihic had a group in Srebrenica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's important, yeah. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an author named Nijaz Masic, author of a book called "Srebrenica: Aggression, Resistance, Treason, Genocide," written in July of 1999?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of that author. I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you an extract from the book. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, we will be -- I'll be seeking to tender this into evidence. It's been disclosed to the Defence. If you want the full book tendered or if the Defence do, we can do so in due course but at the moment I only have an extract that I want to produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a position on this, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no, I have not, because we only were informed this morning that an excerpt from the book will be used today in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't answer my question. Whether you want -- you're satisfied with only this excerpt being in the records or whether you require the entire book to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The excerpt for now, Your Honour. I haven't seen the book yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, thank you. It's on Sanction, if Your Honours please, the computer. Okay. Now, look I don't need to take you through this chapter and verse but if you look at the B/C/S version there in your language, you'll see at the top right-hand page -- top right-hand portion of the page there is a long number and the B/C/S version should end with the number 657. Do you see that? I'll be grateful if Madam -- Ms. Usher could assist by pointing out the --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Good. All right. Now, if you turn over the page to the part 661 and then turn it over once again to the part 662, please? MR. DI FAZIO: And Your Honours will see that you've got a corresponding English with the same number, English translation. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this author says that there is a number of people who assisted him. It's about midway down the page. And he expresses special gratitude to a number of people, presumably for writing his book and just cast your eye down the list of people there. Now, do you recognise some of the names of people who assisted him in the writing of the book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio. Is there a reason why some of the names are in bold and the rest aren't? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: Not that I'm aware of. I don't think it corresponds with the -- oh, no, no. You can see in the B/C/S version they are in bold too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but do you know of any reason? MR. DI FAZIO: No, I don't. I don't know of any reason. None that springs to mind anyway. I certainly don't know of any reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, my question is -- you recognise some of those names there, of the people who helped him write the book?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know some of the names, and I will explain it here now. The book was written by -- well, actually a number of people wrote books and everybody felt certain sympathies towards some people and they wanted to perhaps glorify or commend somebody. But I know exactly what happened out in the field and perhaps Mr. Masic wanted to say something like that. For example, I know Mr. Malkic, Dzevad. He's from Poznanovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Rahman also. So I know these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that some of the people here, mentioned here, are extremely well-placed to provide a history of events in 1992 in the Srebrenica area? Because they were there. You'd have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that each one was in a position to present some situation from the conflict, but I know exactly what happened out in the field and what happened as for Nijaz Masic, I don't know whether the people provided these explanations to him or not. That's something that I don't know. Mr. Masic could have put the names in the book regardless of whether he spoke to them or not. For example, I mentioned Malkic, Dzevad and Rahman Malkic. These are people that I know but I know nor a fact that he was actually never in that area. He never came there in order to be able to describe a situation in the same way that I could describe it. Because I was there and I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Okay. But you would agree that whether they could speak about all of the events in Srebrenica or some of the events, these people who are listed here are people who are well-placed to speak about aspects, at the very least, of what happened in Srebrenica in 1992 and early 1993? That's all. Not whether Mr. Masic did go out and speak with him, not whether he held conferences with them. Not asking that. A very simple question. You would agree that these people are in a good position to speak to him about aspects of events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, is that all the people, the 50 names or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to pass a comment on this, to remark to Mr. Di Fazio but. MR. DI FAZIO: Look, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is predicated on the fact that he knows each and every one of them and their knowledge of the events and their presence or their being able to -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll move on. Thank you, Your Honours. I take your point. I'll withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because even if he said yes, I would rather take it with a pinch of salt. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dzevad Malkic halfway down the list there's a man there, Dzevad Malkic, right next to the name Abdurahman -- Abdurahman Malkic. Now, that's the gentleman who was -- you mentioned yesterday in evidence. Do you remember his name? Dzevad Malkic. Right. Now I think you'd agree that he at least is in a good position -- you'd agree, wouldn't you, that he's in a good position to be able to describe events in your area in 1992 to the author. Not whether he did, but that he's in a good position to describe the events to the author?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he was in the position. All of those who were out in the field, perhaps they were able to tell the author about what happened. Whether he did that or not, I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you for that answer. Now, would you move on, please, to turn over the pages of the B/C/S and you'll get to the text of the -- of the book itself, or, rather, a selection, and if you look for that familiar number at the top right-hand page you'll see it ends in the number 744 and it's talking about Osmace. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. All right. Could I ask you, please, to -- to read from about halfway down the first page, where it begins with the words, "We could breathe easier when the Skelani unit led by Ahmo Tihic was formed in the end of May 1992." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if you just cast your eye over what the author says about Skelani and Mr. Tihic and Poznanovici and those villages that you can see mentioned there, thereunder. Just read it. Read it carefully because then I have some questions about it for you. Okay. Have you -- you've had a chance to look at it and read it.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, firstly, the author says that we, presumably the Bosniak population, could breathe easier when Skelani, the Skelani unit led by Ahmo Tihic was formed in the end of May 1992. Firstly, my first question is this: Have you ever heard of such an event or do you have any knowledge of such an event, the formation of a Skelani unit formed end of May 1992, led by Ahmo Tihic? I'm sure you could answer that with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage, I did not know about the setting up of that unit by the end of May. I said that I found out after the demilitarisation of Srebrenica that that group had been formed and that he was leader of that group, the group of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Skelani from Poznanovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Further, you go down, and it says that soldiers from Osmace Kragljivoda, Biljeg, Skenderovici, and Stari Grad helped in the destruction of Chetnik strongholds in Ratkovici, and it mentions these hamlets, Polinci, Ducici, Dvorista, and Brdjani. My first question is: Are you aware of any soldiers from those places mentioned there helping in the destruction of Chetnik strongholds in the Ratkovici area? This combination of soldiers from all of those areas? Did you ever hear of any such event?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with that. I said that there was no coordination here. There wasn't a situation of a number of units acting together. I said that it was a spontaneous response to what we went through at those times in our area and we had -- very many refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I heard -- I know what you said yesterday. I'm not -- I -- and I heard it. But if there had been a -- if there had been a -- what's the word -- coming together of soldiers from Osmace, Kragljivoda, Biljeg, Skenderovici, and Stari Grad to assist in the destruction of a Chetnik stronghold in Ratkovici on the 21st of June 1992, you'd have to agree wouldn't you that you'd be in a mighty fine position to be able to tell the Trial Chamber about it? You'd have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that there was coordination of units, that there was concerted effort. We did have refugees from a number of different villages. That means from Voljavica, Zaluzje, Abdulici, Zanjevo, Skelani, et cetera. All those were people who were refugees. They were in the woods. And it was a spontaneous attack and those people just came along and I'm not arguing against the fact that there were people from many different places but there was no coordination. If only we could have had that coordination, if only we could have had the situation like that, we would not have experienced the horrific things that we had experienced like people having to live outdoors for 10 days and the fight for sheer life. And it was a matter of hours in which it was decided whether you were going to live or not. So it was a simple response to what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just before I -- before I return to this issue, you just said something that interests me. You said that if -- you said that you didn't have that coordination and that if only we could have had that coordination, if only we could have had a situation like that, we would not have experienced the horrific things that we experienced. I'm right, aren't I, that based on what you experienced in 1992, coordination would have assisted greatly in resisting Serb forces? Would you agree with that? That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean about the Serb forces. Could you please repeat your question once again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not really asking you about Serb forces. I'm asking you about what you said a few seconds ago. You said that there was no coordination. "If only we could have had that coordination, if only we could have had the situation like that, we would not have experienced the horrific things that we experienced." So you're saying, aren't you, that coordination between different groupings of fighters or soldiers, as this book seems to be talking about, that sort of coordination, that sort of acting together, would really have helped you in the situation that you faced in those months in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So what I'm saying is that there was no coordination and I did say that that attack came about in a spontaneous way due to the situation that we were in. So I can confirm that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hate interrupting you but I think reading this paragraph, I would draw a distinction between coordination, which arises out of the reply that he gave, and collaboration. That seems to be the appropriate description of what you have alleged in this paragraph. The fact that you have -- MR. DI FAZIO: All right, I'm happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the soldiers from Osmace, Kragljivoda, Biljeg, Skenderovici, helped in the destruction of Chetnik stronghold, does not necessarily involve coordination but it does certainly involve collaboration. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right? So what is more important, I think, to know, is whether he agrees that on the 21st of June 1992, when this fighting described here allegedly took place, he is aware that there were soldiers, and this is not refugees that the book is talking about, but soldiers from Osmace, Kragljivoda, Biljeg, Skenderovici and Stari Grad helping in the destruction of the Chetnik strongholds in Ratkovici. That is all he needs to confirm or reject. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. Certainly I agree with you but my last question was really based on -- purely and simply on the answer that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I mean, I'm not interfering and I'm pointing this out because when he mentioned refugees giving a hand Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. spontaneously, it so happens that they are described as coming from other places, completely different places to these. So this is why I'm asking you or I'm pointing these out because it's not fair to ask the question to the witness whether there was coordination or organised coordination. I mean, coordination implies organised coordination. He never said that there was organised coordination. And neither does the book, at least that's the way I read it. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay I'll ask the question Your Honour proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not asking the witness a question myself. I'm just pointing out -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll put it nice and simple, really easy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know, did you see, are you aware of, any soldiers -- I mean soldier, that's what the book says, I use the word soldier, from those places, Osmace, Biljeg, Skenderovici, Stari Grad, et cetera, helping in the destruction of the Chetnik strong hold in Ratkovici on the 21st of June, 1992. That's simplicity itself, I think. So are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I said that there were thousands of refugees and amongst those refugees -- well, we can't rule out the fact that there may have been individuals amongst them who participated in all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The author then -- sorry, the last question the one that I should ask you is: Okay. Now that I've led you to what this author has to say about the issue, does that affect your evidence in any way? Or in other words, does that change your mind about what you've said, and bear in mind you don't have to change your mind because of what someone wrote in a book. But now that I've taken you to a section and you've thought about it and you've seen what this fellow has to say about it, does that alter your evidence in any respect?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need the Prosecutor to repeat the question because it is unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Look. I'm just trying to be fair to you. What I'm asking you is this: I've showed you this little bit in the book, all right? About what happened in Ratkovici on the 21st of June and about these other fighters from these other places. That's what the book says, and we've heard what you've had to say about the issue. All I'm asking you is simply this: Now that I've taken you to the book, showed you what this author says, do you want to change your evidence regarding who participated in events at Ratkovici? By that, I mean soldiers. Or do you stand firm with your evidence from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand firm to what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Read on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because you have to be fair. I'm not saying that you're being unfair, but don't misread me. But having read this, I know that you have told us that you were not aware of any soldiers from Osmace, Kragljivoda, Biljeg, Skenderovici helping in the destruction, et cetera. Do you exclude the possibility or would you agree that it could have possibly happened but you are not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I mentioned thousands and thousands of refugees, and amongst all those people, it can't really be ruled out that such people were there and that they went in search for food and so on. But I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the way the question was framed and the answer given, would have excluded this statement that he has just made. MR. DI FAZIO: I think we are all clear now and the witness's position is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not denying that this ever happened. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, he's not denying that the people from those places may be present. He certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And with regard to the destruction of the Chetnik stronghold in Ratkovici he certainly hasn't allowed that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not dealing with that, Mr. Jones. We are dealing -- because the question seemed to have put in contrast his testimony with what is written here and in actual fact it is not in contrast or not necessarily in contrast. Let's put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. For the destruction he's spoken he has ruled that out, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you ready with this document? MR. DI FAZIO: Just one more aspect of it and then I'll tender it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read on. The author then goes to describe the inner liberation of this island in Poznanovici was finished on the 30th of June during the fight for the destruction of the Chetnik stronghold in Brezani, and how -- goes on to describe how the Chetniks from president any were harming passengers through the forest - that might mean travellers - between the island where Bosniaks from Osmace, Poznanovici, Skenderovici and so on were squeezed. And it goes on to say that all formed combat units are participating in the combats due to the strength of the Chetnik stronghold. The fights are personally led by Srebrenica TO commander Naser Oric. Do you see that? That portion of the book.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You agree, don't you, that Osmace --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree because there was no proper line of command there in the beginning of 1992, and until the end of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My question is simply this: The author is clearly talking about fighting in this area up to the period of June, 30th of June 1992 and he says, the author says that the fights are personally led by Mr. Oric. Now, in the time that you were in the area in 1992, did you see or did you become aware of Mr. Oric ever personally leading these fights?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never witnessed that myself, Naser leading any combat activities, nor did I hear from anyone that there was any formal command either in the beginning of 1992 or during the summer, that there was any command as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's the next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P566, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will become Prosecution Exhibit P566. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Could I seek your indulgence at this point, if Your Honours please? It's 20 past. It would help me at this stage because I'm waiting some other information and that will help me streamline matters for later in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Would 25 minutes be enough? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, in fact, I want -- yes, I certainly wouldn't want it any longer. I need the time. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before my colleague Di Fazio continues, I would just like to state for the transcript the following. I just had the opportunity to look at the section of the book and the translation of that part provided to us by the Prosecutor and that is the reason why I talked about this with the Prosecution this morning. We don't want to receive translations like this. There are some very serious mistakes in the translation. I can -- which could lead the Trial Chamber to a completely different conclusion about the facts that are stated here. For example, I've noticed now that on page 93 of this part of the book, the Prosecutor used this morning, referring to Osmace, this part which the Prosecutor used saying it was easier to breathe in the end of May 1992, the third sentence in the Bosnian says, "In the fight for the liquidation of Chetnik strongholds in Ratkovici," but as it is translated it says "the soldiers from Osmace, Kragljivoda, Skenderovici and Stari Grad helped in the destruction of the Chetnik strongholds." In our language and I think in the English too the word "liquidation of strongholds" has a completely different meaning. Liquidation can mean to neutralise, to drive away, to -- so, to liquidate a stronghold does not mean to destroy or demolish it. So I would like the witness to clarify that, and am I right when I say this? And I would ask that in future we do not receive translations in the middle of the proceedings because then we cannot really be monitoring the proceedings and looking for things that could be of help to our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that the witness was not reading the English version and was reading the B/C/S version so there is no question of he being at least misled or having the problem of confusing "destruction" with "liquidation."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just add something as an English speaker, because it was something which I pointed out and discussed with my colleague. The indictment obviously charges among other things destruction of Ratkovici. This translation refers to Ratkovici being destroyed when in the Bosnian we say it's a different word, it's "liquidation" or "elimination." That's why obviously it's of paramount importance to us that it be corrected. That's the point, really. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, we've had "liquidation" and now "elimination" as well. Perhaps the Defence can make up their mind. But in any event, I'm not going to quibble over a word like liquidation. Liquidation suits me just fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is that the witness had in front of him the original. MR. DI FAZIO: The B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The B/C/S, yes, which says [B/C/S spoken] so I don't see where the confusion arises because that's what he had. We were using the word "destruction" because that's what we had in the translation and I acknowledge that the word "destruction" has a different connotation from "liquidation."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution agrees "liquidation." Let's just correct the English translation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not agreeing anything. The only people who can tell you what the meaning of the word is are the people in the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would move ahead, Mr. Jones, because basically what we have here is a book. The author is not here giving evidence. It's Mr. Ramic who is giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he had the word liquidation in his -- in front of him, not destruction. So -- at the end of the day what we are going to look at is not the really the book but at his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please try to finish by quarter to 2.00. MR. DI FAZIO: I will do my level best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that you can do it, if necessary by kangaroo leaps. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to turn to another topic Mr. Ramic. I just want to remind you of some of your evidence from yesterday concerning the issue of weaponry. You recall, don't you, that you -- your position was that, at least in I think April or May of 1992, you people in Poznanovici only had about five or six hunting rifles and pistols. Do you remember that evidence? All I'm asking you is do you remember it? I'm sure you can answer it yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also said that there were also a number -- there was also a number of homemade -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition so bad was your situation vis-a-vis weaponry that the man Blagoje Prodanovic drunkenly when he was affected by alcohol, tried to give you an automatic weapon out of some sort of sympathy at your position because of the lack of weaponry. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And furthermore, other points that you made in your evidence yesterday were that you yourself only had a pistol, a legal -- legally held pistol, and some of your fellow villagers were so pressed by this lack of weaponry that they had to manufacture crude rifles which were so bad they shot backwards on some occasions. Do you agree with those two -- did you recall those two features of your evidence, your pistol and being forced to manufacture crude rifles?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition, you said when you were asked about your -- about you and Mr. Dzevad Malkic, that -- whether you were a military unit, according to what you know about military units, and you went on to say you didn't have adequate weapons, uniforms, and no ammunition. I want to be fair to you. Were you saying yesterday that you, you the people yourself, Mr. Malkic and the villagers from your village, had no ammunition whatsoever or were you really meaning to say, look, you had very little ammunition?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a small amount of ammunition for the small number of weaponry. These were very small quantities of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you for that clarification. Now, there was no other way for any ammunition or weaponry to get to you because of the isolation of the various Muslim villages, not only isolation from each other but isolation from Srebrenica. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about Poznanovici, Podkorjen, Dedici, and Karici, we were these four villages, small hamlets, actually; we were not isolated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from those, you drew a map yesterday. I don't know if I need to show it to you but you remember drawing a map and circling all the villages. You circled some in a dark blue and some in a dark green. Do you remember that? Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I don't need to show it to the witness but your purpose yesterday was to show that those villages which you circled which you identified as Muslim villages, your purpose -- not your purpose but what you said was that those were isolated from each other and certainly from Srebrenica. Do you recall that evidence? I think you said --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you'd have to agree, wouldn't you, that there was no way that weaponry could be brought into your areas, into those areas of those Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you were left with very small amount of weaponry, with virtually no ammunition, correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Small quantities of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the months of May, June, July, August, September, is it your position that the same situation applied, namely no source of weaponry coming to you from other Bosniak-held areas?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on the 8th of June, the attack on Podkorjen, we captured an automatic rifle and ammunition. This was on the 8th of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One? One automatic rifle? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just turn to another topic briefly. You -- is it your position that your villages around Poznanovici, the Muslim villages, were being shelled prior to the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were shelled before the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that the Serbs cut off the electricity on the 8th of June. You were specific about that date. Did the Serbs permit the supply of electricity to come through to you whilst they were shelling you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the electricity was cut on the 8th of June. Until the 8th of June we did have electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood you and you've just confirmed that I understood you correctly. I'm not quibbling with what you said and that's what you said yesterday. So you had a supply of electricity to the -- up until the 8th of June when it was cut, and you were being shelled by the Serbs prior to the 8th of June. You must agree, therefore, don't you, that the Serbs did not cut or at least permitted the supply of electricity to reach your villages as they were shelling you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we had electricity up until the 8th of June but there was shelling, yes there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear enough, I think. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, let's move on. I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you now to turn to the events of the 8th of June, and you gave evidence about that yesterday, describing it. Essentially what happened was this: If -- and you correct me if I'm wrong. On the 8th of June, those young boys that you had up on that hill, that elevation, can't remember the name, saw Serb army movements and they reported it to people in your village. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your conclusion was that there was an imminent Serb attack. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confirming the killing of our people on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. But what I'm -- I understood your evidence from yesterday to be quite apart from killings on the road, I'm not asking you about that but I understood your evidence to be that the boys up on the hill or the elevation saw the Serbs, Serb army, and reported -- reported to you that fact, from which you concluded there was an attack about to take place. Now, is that fair enough? Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did know because they tried several times to carry out infantry attacks against us before the 8th of June. That is how we concluded and knew that they would attack us, because the shelling was on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suspect the interpreters may want to raise a matter or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was just that His Honour left his microphone on. That was all. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm not asking you about attacks prior to the 8th of June. I'm asking you about the 8th of June because you gave lots of evidence about that yesterday. So let's stick to the 8th of June. Let's focus on the 8th of June. You said - all I'm asking you is recapping what you said and I don't want to misquote you, I don't want to put words in your mouth. All I'm trying to say is the essence of what you said yesterday is this: The boys are up on the higher elevation, it's the 8th of June, they see the Serbs, they report that fact. You men in your village concluded with that report from the boys, well, the Serbs, they are going to attack us. Is that fair or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. How could they conclude that? We didn't know what they were thinking. We could just assume that perhaps there would be an attack. But we didn't know. It was logical that we didn't know. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just read out your evidence to you from yesterday. Page 51. Question by Madam Vidovic: "Do you remember specifically any one of those observers that you talked to, any one of the people who were looking at it? Yes, I do remember a boy called Hamid" - I can't read the surname - "who informed us that the Serb army was moving from the direction of Fakovici, Ratkovici, and Ducici, and they had already come as far as" -- and I -- again the transcript is not clear. My memory is that it's some odd-sounding name like Metaljka. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it was 700 metres away. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you concluded that there was an attack imminent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he -- he has answered that question. He said that you -- they thought about it but they did not conclude it. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You decided to do something about it, didn't you, because you took action, didn't you? Moving the population up into the woods for safety, one of the first moves that you made. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't take the population to the woods. They always did that spontaneously on their own. We couldn't move the population somewhere else. There were thousands of them. How could I have done that? It always happened spontaneously, when the shelling happened, with all the shells, and then after the killing, I don't want to mention the names of the people. After that we decided to put up a resistance so that they wouldn't enter the village. That was the whole point of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, then. Did the boys go around telling the rest of the population that were gathered there of the Serb movements?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the population spontaneously went to the woods, and when the firing stopped, then some people would go and cross over and ask what had happened, ask the refugees. Our boys just actually monitored every day the movements of the Serbian soldiers, but they didn't coordinate the movements of the refugees because that was something that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you couldn't control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea, can you tell the Trial Chamber, how the civilians decided upon going up to take refuge in the woods?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have any idea? Well, fear and everything that others in other villages experienced before them was sufficient for them to run to the woods. They weren't going to wait to be slaughtered and raped and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But in order to avoid being slaughtered and raped, so on, they had to know that the Serbs were coming to slaughter and rape them, correct? And the only way they could know that would have been from the boys telling them or someone who had been told from the -- by the boys telling them of the imminent arrival of the Serb forces and the danger of slaughter and rape. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The citizens had contacts with the refugees, which were spread out from Voljavica to Skelani. There were thousands of them and those people talked. They found out. They knew what was going on. They knew who was expelled from each village. There was no need for them to receive information from any boys or scouts. People just knew. The Serb army always started with the artillery first, that's how they would cleanse the terrain, and then they would attack so that a sign for the refugees to leave during the shelling and to expect an attack was that. It happened countless of times that there would be shelling. Perhaps it wasn't an infantry attack but they would be sleeping in the woods. They got sick because they stayed in the woods because they didn't dare to sleep in the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to another aspect of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you move to another aspect, if the -- as you said, the information given to you by the boy -- this boy Hamid or other boys that were with him, namely that the Serb forces had arrived already up to Metaljka which you described was only 700 metres away, would the population in your village have been able to see the Serb forces with the naked eyes at that distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village -- well, let me explain. You couldn't see it from the village because that part -- actually the area of Metaljka that I was describing is under the -- under trees now. It's forested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That eliminates the possibility of them having actually seen the forces at Metaljka. Okay. You can move to another -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to Metaljka itself. Your position from yesterday, as I understand your evidence, was that the boys came and informed you of this imminent Serb -- well, I won't use those words again. The boys came and informed you of the Serb movement. You had a meeting and you decided to meet the Serbs at the point described as Metaljka and to offer resistance. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We decided to put up a resistance in order to save the people. Actually, after the killing of two of our men on the road to Podkorjen. They were killed and we decided to put up a resistance so that they could not enter further into the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who made that decision? The decision to offer resistance and the decision to offer that resistance at the point called Metaljka.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already we had a group of volunteers, and after these events, in talks with those men who were there, the young men who were there, the decision was made right then and there to go after Metaljka. I participated directly in those talks there, when the agreement was reached. There was no special order. Simply the events that were unfolding, that these people were killed and that they would go to the village, then those of us who had some weapons, we came out and what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But it's very -- I understand what you're saying but all I want to know is this: Was there a commander who decided to offer resistance and was there a commander who decided to offer resistance at the point called Metaljka? Or was that just the subject of a discussion amongst the men and eventually you reached agreement?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no commander. There was no word of any kind of commander. I was there all the time, and this boy was telling me, he was giving me information, and I and a group of our men made this decision. There was nobody particular ordering or who could issue such an order, simply those who wanted to go went in an effort to save people. Nobody could issue orders to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It was -- I'm sure you can answer this with a yes or a no. Was Dzevad Malkic present at this discussion?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was present. Dzevad Malkic and some other young men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone come up with an alternative approach to the problem? For example, retreating, fleeing, offering a resistance at a place different from Metaljka? Did anyone have any other view about the matter?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this happened spontaneously, and there wasn't much time to think. There were no alternatives, simply the area of Podkorjen was there and it was about 7 to 8 kilometres away from Serbian villages, from Ratkovici, so there was no need to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday you answering questions from Madam Vidovic about this episode, and you answered, page 53, "Well, we resolved to get organised, to organise the weapons that we had and to go out to Metaljka, to wait for the Serb forces, in order to give the opportunity to the inhabitants, that is, to flee to the woods." Madam Vidovic asked you, "Right, and what happened after that?" You answered, "Well, the population managed to get to the woods and we managed to surprise the Serbs by going out to meet them at Metaljka. And there was fierce fighting there. And the Serbs were somewhat surprised. The Serb military were surprised. And they had to withdraw again in the direction of Ratkovici and a number of other villages in the direction of Fakovici." And you went on to say there was hand-to-hand fighting. Close quarters anyway. So do I understand your evidence correctly that the Metaljka point was selected in order to provide the people with the best means of taking refuge up in the -- up in the woods?
