utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That road led to the village of Podkorjen. And that's why the objective was to stop the Serbian soldiers or the Serbian army there, because if they passed that place, they would practically be entering the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not aware of anyone telling or informing the Serbs -- sorry, the civilians who were with you, to flee to the woods while we fighters maintain a hold -- an action -- a holding action at Metaljka in order to prevent them from getting to you, to prevent the Serbs from getting to you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I won't. I'll withdraw the question. The Serbs that you went out to meet at the point at Metaljka were armed, you said, with automatic rifles, machine-guns and a machine-gun with a calibre 84, which was the first time that you'd seen such a weapon. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I mentioned that that was the first time that I saw an 84-calibre machine-gun, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Pardon my ignorance but is that a somewhat more powerful machine-gun, quite a bigger, more effective weapon than a usual machine-gun, say a Kalashnikov or something like that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a much more lethal weapon than a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And furthermore, following the events on the 8th of June, when you went out and searched the area where the fighting had been, you came across a gentleman who you knew as -- I don't know his full name. I can't tell from the transcript but I think his surname was Markovic and he was also called Bato. You remember describing that man, you found his body?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, he -- okay. He was a Serb, first of all, wasn't he, killed in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he was really impressively armed, wasn't he? He --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had -- let's go through what he had. He had camouflage uniform a bullet proof vest, automatic rifle, quite a few bombs, ammunition, incendiaries, and fragmentation ammunition. Do you remember all of that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see quite a number of other Serb fighters also as impressively and heavily armed as Mr. -- as this fellow Bato?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw an 84. They had machine-guns, they had automatic weapons, most of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you managed to defeat those Serbs armed with your weapons, didn't you? That's your evidence to this Trial Chamber. At least on that day, in that encounter. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor is saying to defeat them. I don't recall saying that we defeated anyone. One Serb fighter was killed and they withdrew. They were surprised and there was a withdrawal, but I don't know about defeating them. I'm sure that there were some fighters who did stay in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- you said yesterday that the Serbs were somewhat surprised, the Serb military were surprised, and they had to withdraw again in the direction of Ratkovici. Is it your position that upon encountering resistance from you, which caused the surprise, they simply turned around and got out of the places as best they could? Out of the area where this action was taking place.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't leave. They actually ran off. They fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dropping their ammunition and weapons as they went, which you later collected from the field, correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. We found a lot of ammunition, anti-infantry grenades, well, I don't need to list them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you go into this action armed with a pistol that you possessed, the legally held pistol, the one that you told us about earlier?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a pistol, and I went with this pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have anything else matching what the Serbs had on that particular day, automatic rifles, this big machine-gun with the 84-calibre machine-gun? You didn't have that, did you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Did the Serbs manage to use their 84-calibre machine-gun in the hand-to-hand or close-quarter fighting?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They used it for a long time in the course of their withdrawal. They were covering themselves during the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the rifles that sometimes shot out backwards, were they used during this particular encounter on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand the question. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can clarify it for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about weapons that, the paucity of weapons and how you were forced or some people were forced in your area to construct crude rifles that sometimes blew -- sorry, shot backwards. My question is this: On the 8th of June at this encounter that we are talking about, were those rifles that shot -- occasionally shot backwards used?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those rifles were used, pistols, the homemade weapons were used, yes. Had we had better ones, we wouldn't have had to use those ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any Serbs taken prisoner on that day, that you saw or are aware of?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody was captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that -- I'll withdraw that. The Serbs, not only had on that particular -- in that particular encounter the sort of weaponry that we have been talking about, the 84-calibre machine-gun and machine-guns and automatic rifles, but they also had to use horses to transport heavy weaponry. What sort of heavy weaponry was being transported on the horses on that day, and did they -- were they able to use that heavy weaponry in the fight?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had those 84 machine-guns which are quite heavy and they needed the horses for those machine-guns and mortars. All their logistical support, ammunition, I suppose. I said that there was a distance of 16 kilometres to Fakovici so it was a certain distance to be reckoned with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave the 8th of June and move to the 12th of June. All I want to do is once again just remind you of your evidence. You said yesterday, didn't you, that on the 12th of June - that's about four days later - the Serbs attacked and destroyed a good part of Poznanovici. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that caused the population in your village and neighbouring villages to take -- to take to the forests, take to the woods, for -- presumably for safety, where they remained until the 21st of June. That's what you said yesterday, and do you agree with that now?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so -- and that was -- I think you went on to give some detailed evidence about how that was an unpleasant period of time because of being forced out into the open and all of the things that happened to the people in that period of time. You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the -- on the 21st of May -- of June, you once again saw Serb forces approaching you; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so from your position -- I mean your position personally and the civilians, and any of the men who had weapons up in the forests, from that position, you decided to -- people amongst you decided that you had no more choice and now was the time to go and confront the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save the people at all costs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So that's what I want to know. So it was -- the people are gathered up in the woods, somehow the Serbs are seen approaching, and from that place in the woods, the people decide to go and confront the approaching Serb forces. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we set off to save the people, the civilians realised that the time had come to do something, that we could no longer continue as we were, and they followed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And they followed you and they were carrying axes and saws, they were crazed, it was a terrible sight, and they were banging on pots and pans. Now, from what you could see and observe, that's what a Serb soldier or one of the members of the Serb armed forces that were advancing towards you, that's what he or -- he would have seen, a mass of people carrying axes, saws, banging on pots and pans. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether it's correct or not, I wouldn't say that, but yes, it could have been seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What was the purpose of the banging of the pots and the pans?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that people were crazed. They were almost out of their minds altogether. They had spent 10 days outdoors in the woods. I don't want to go into that description once again because I find it really hard, but they said it was all or nothing at that stage, the lack of food, the constant shelling, the wounds, the murders. People were out of their minds. And they could simply not carry on under that much pressure on a daily basis and there was no way out. And I really don't like talking about this because I find it really hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understand.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because as I said my children were there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that. And I'm not taking issue with the bad conditions that you've been talking about. My question is simply this: It's the banging of the pots and pans. Do you have any idea why that was occurring?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it all started in a spontaneous manner. After everything that people had experienced in the period prior to that, they just rose up and nobody actually gave any pots and pans to anyone to bang them together or give them any other implements that could have been used as weapons because there was no time for that. But it was simply not the time where we had the opportunity to give advice to anyone. It was all very spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that the banging of pots and pans was certainly not to alert the Serb forces as to your presence, would you agree with me? And furthermore, would you agree with me that the banging of pots and pans was something intended to scare the Serbs and coordinated with the men who had guns? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. It wasn't coordinated with any group of fighters. There was no coordination whatsoever because we actually tried to get them to come back, not to go. But to keep thousands of homeless and hungry people under control was simply impossible. The only thing we could have done was shoot them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection is that this -- that was a compound question which guaranteed to get a confused answer, and my concern is that it might look like the witness was not answering the question about whether it was intended to scare the Serbs. If the witness can just be asked was the banging of pots and pans intended to scare the Serbs, I think the answer is pretty obvious. But he slipped in whether it was coordinated, and of course the witness answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was the only question I would have put in the first place or I would have put it in the first place before -- MR. DI FAZIO: All right okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go direct and put the question because if you ask him whether they were banging to alert the Serbs as to their presence, I mean, come on. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no. Well, I respectfully agree with what Your Honour observes. I will just be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The banging of the pots and pans was not designed to alert the Serbs as to your position, was it?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not designed to alert them. It just rose up spontaneously, and as to what happened later, most probably there was just too much fear on the part of a whole -- especially when they saw this mass of people, and that frightened them and that's why they started to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the next issue that I want to -- your evidence was that the Serb soldiers -- you saw the Serb soldiers approaching and -- sorry, the Serb soldiers saw the people approaching and they simply started to withdraw, to run away and to throw down their weapons. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the Serb soldiers taking out their weapons, fleeing into the distance?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any shots fired? Did they, for instance, try to shoot the people who were banging on the pots and pans or fire bullets at the people who were banging on the pots and pans or indeed any of the men who may have been lucky enough to have --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what the witness has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to repeat the question and the witness needs to repeat his answer because the interpreters didn't catch what you answered, actually. So please repeat the question for the benefit of the witness. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb forces try and shoot at the people who were banging on the pots and pans or any of the men amongst those people who were lucky enough to be armed?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did, but as this mass of people came closer, they realised that they were advancing anyway, and then they started to run away and throw their weapons and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what numbers of people were mown down by the Serbs, if any?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few wounded and quite a few people killed but this whole mass of people paid no heed. They just decided to continue to the bitter end and, as I said, it was very difficult to keep thousands and thousands of refugees under control. The situation was such as to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to spend too much more time on this. Let's move along. Just one more thing could you confirm for me the Serbs not only turned and ran but they didn't take their weapons with them, they threw them on the ground, or at least some of them did? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an opinion on my part. I just saw some people dropping their weapons. Of course they did not throw any light weapons away but if you have a heavy weapon, it is not easy to run carrying that weapon. So it wasn't always the same. I mean some of the Serb soldiers did drop their weapons and others didn't. But I did see some of them do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do I take it from that answer that the Serbs had some heavy weaponry with which they could confront this mass of civilians?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had machine-guns and mortars, and entire infantry weapons as well. So they did have heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many guns would you say, rifles, would you say were amongst -- were possessed by the mass of people advancing on these Serbs? How many weapons? Have you got any idea?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of my group. We had about ten rifles within our group. That's a rough assessment. Well, it was quite some time ago, Your Honour, so almost 13 years ago, and it is a bit difficult to remember every single detail, but we must have had about ten rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Anyway, the -- you also said that the next Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stage in events on that day was that you managed to get down to Gornji Ratkovici and that there was some resistance from the Serbs in the houses but that they eventually withdrew back towards Fakovici. You remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So was there house-to-house fighting in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it Fakovici or -- MR. DI FAZIO: My apologies, thank you, Your Honour. I misled the witness and my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I misled you. Was there house-to-house fighting in Gornji Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I got to Gornji Ratkovici and the Serb army was firing from the houses, so there was a fight and then the Serb forces withdrew. Whether it was out of fear before this mass of refugees after a certain period of time they withdrew. But I did see that they were firing from the houses, from the barns and stables, from the village itself, and around the village, there were some trenches there at about 15 metres away from the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The result is the Serbs leave the village, the Bosniak or Muslim fighters make their way into the village, which has been vacated, correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, the people went into the village and this group of fighters simply went in very fast and then they got out quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We'll get on it that in a moment but the fact of the matter is, isn't it, that you were able to drive out these Serbs from Gornji Ratkovici with some house to house fighting without the place burning down, correct? Or suffering large fire damage? I'm not asking you about what happened later with the bombing. I'm talking about that early part. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This house-to-house fighting that you are mentioning, I don't -- reading the transcript and following what the witness has said, he's said that there was shooting from the houses but at no time did he say, at least to my recollection, that there was house-to-house fighting. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. I'll just -- I'll deal with that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, you can deal with it because there may have been, I don't know that but I don't recollect the witness saying that there was house-to-house fighting. I recollect you, of course, mentioning it but ... MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can clear this up. MR. DI FAZIO: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked questions by Madam Vidovic about this, precisely this, and she asked you, "And how far did you get to?" And you answered, "I got to Gornji Ratkovici close to Gornji Ratkovici. At that point I couldn't continue because there was fire from a machine-gun from the houses. Automatic weapons fire from the houses. So we couldn't approach the village -- villages. They were firing at us. We were firing at them. I said that I had a pistol with me at the time. At the time we just couldn't get any closer. They were firing mostly from the houses. There were also some trenches but it was from the trenches that were about 15 metres from the houses." Now, by that answer, did you mean that there was house-to-house fighting or simply that the Serbs resisted from inside Gornji Ratkovici and then suddenly vacated it without any house-to-house fighting? What --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was withdrawal. As to whether there was any fighting from the distance that I was at, I can't tell very accurately. I wasn't able to tell whether there was actually house-to-house fighting as such, but as to the fact that there was fighting from where I was, I did see their action, their machine-guns in action, and I could see them firing, and afterwards, I saw that they withdrew and as to there was actual house-to-house fighting, I could not say with 100 per cent certainty because I myself did not participate in any house-to-house fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, one thing is clear. You Muslim Bosniak fighters wanted to get into Ratkovici, Gornji Ratkovici, and the Serbs who were in Gornji Ratkovici wanted to keep you out. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they tried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, in the course of that, and up until the time the Serbs finally left Gornji Ratkovici, Gornji Ratkovici did not catch fire. Is that your position? Is that what you say happened?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was no fire. I mentioned in my statement that I saw a barn on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber what the purpose was in going into Gornji Ratkovici, engaging in this fighting to get into Gornji Ratkovici, bearing in mind your earlier evidence that this whole action on the 21st of June was just a spontaneous reaction to approaching Serb forces? Do you -- do you know how -- why was that part of your spontaneous reaction, to go into Gornji Ratkovici? Or did it just happen that way?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our top priority was to get food. The people were starving, and also, because there were quite a few of us who were homeless, we thought that it would be very handy for some of them to move into those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you see, you've told us, you told the Trial Chamber this morning that -- and yesterday, that all these events on the 21st of June 1992, all of what happened, all the fighting that you're talking about, was a spontaneous thing that suddenly occurred when these -- this mass of unfortunate people saw the oncoming Serbs. It was just a spontaneous thing. There was no planning to it, was there? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that it was a spontaneous thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fight, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. All right. Now, if it was a spontaneous fight, was the entrance, the fighting, to get into Gornji Ratkovici, part of that spontaneous reaction or was it something that was decided upon at some other point in time?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a part of that spontaneous action, the entry into the village was part of that spontaneous action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the issue of it being handy for you to move into those houses? Was that discussed on the 21st of June amongst the fighters? Or amongst -- sorry, I won't use that word. Amongst the Muslim men who were armed and who were engaged in this action at Gornji Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, later on, there were talks after the 21st of July [as interpreted] that those homeless people could be moved into those houses, that that could be used as accommodation, and on the 21st of June, in fact, I said that everything was spontaneous. We didn't have time to deal with that. So our entering the village was a part of that spontaneous act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked about -- I'll move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is there a problem Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a part of the answer did not enter the transcript. He said the 21st of June. We did not have time for that. And actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard the interpretation for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did say that. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it is there. It is there. It's line 23 and 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is there. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just while we are on the issue of -- withdraw that. You were asked by Madam Vidovic yesterday this question. You gave this answer. Page 66. "Did you, the people from the villages, Podkorjen and Poznanovici have any interest in setting these houses on fire? Did you have an interest in doing something like that, Mr. Ramic?" And you answered: "No, we had no interest in torching those houses because we had so many people without homes whom we wanted to accommodate in those homes. And Dzevad always said not to destroy this property, that we were not like the Serbs." Now, do you remember that answer -- that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When would Dzevad say to you, not to destroy property, not to destroy Serb homes? When would he say such matters -- such things? What sort of occasions?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our mutual talks, since I knew Dzevad from the very beginning, from the start of the aggression, from the start of the war in May, June, 1992, always, in these contacts, he used to say that we should not destroy property, that it was needed, and we all agreed with what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he wasn't giving you any orders or instructions, he was just raising it as a topic and we all agreed, to quote you.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was just a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to whom did he say these -- these things about not destroying property? I'm only interested in the groupings. Did he give speeches to civilians or was this in conversation with the Muslim or Bosniak men who were armed, such as yourself with your pistol?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking now about contacts between myself and Dzevad, and consultations of that group of ours, the group that -- I mean, you could consider it to be a group of fighters, and I don't know if he spoke with civilians or not. That's a difficult question, and it's hard to give you an answer because it was something that you really couldn't control. If somebody came from Skelani and if Dzevad spoke to some civilians from Potkozeli [phoen] he's not from Skelani, he's not from Voljavica. His house was set on fire from Skelani so he came and he was pretty enraged so in such situations you didn't have the opportunity of -- Dzevad couldn't do it, nor could anybody else, to issue any kind of orders or to control anything that happened later. It would be difficult to control something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to understand you. Am I correct that from what you've said in your answer, that there was an ongoing problem with Serb homes being torched, being burnt down, in your area at least? An ongoing problem that caused Dzevad to talk to you about it from time to time?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about much later, when there were cases when people -- when they went looking for food, would set one house on fire. I'm not ruling out the possibility, but I cannot confirm that. I didn't see it for myself, and I was always against things like that, I myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to, Mr. Ramic, that on the 21st of June 1992, Muslim or Bosniak fighters deliberately and carefully attacked Ratkovici and that, with the help of civilians, the place was looted and burned on that day. Now, I'm just providing you with an opportunity to agree or disagree with me. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go now to the events a little bit later in the day. You said yesterday, and I don't think I'm misquoting you, you said that following the -- your entry into Gornji Ratkovici, you -- sorry. Just bear with me. That you had to leave the area of Gornji Ratkovici and get back to your positions because you expected a Serb counterattack. Do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A counterattack in response to your attack; is that correct? Your attack on Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were afraid because they were constantly attacking us, since 1992, and we were afraid that we would be attacked on that occasion as well. There were several attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Anyway, but you had to get out of the area and get back to your positions because of the expected counterattack, right?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leaving the civilians to go through the town or -- sorry, not town, that's the wrong word. The village, hamlet of Gornji Ratkovici, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about other hamlets clustered nearby? Were the civilians also going through those hamlets and villages, for example, the -- Ratkovici itself, not just Gornji Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it but I assume that the civilians went everywhere after the Serbs withdrew. They would be going there. But there was no control. There was nobody monitoring these movements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And indeed the Serb counterattack took place, according to you, when artillery was fired that day, that afternoon, resulting in the destruction of Ratkovici from Serb bombs and the killing of many -- the indiscriminate killing of many civilians in the area, who were in Ratkovici. That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber why you did not warn the civilians to evacuate the area and get to safer positions, if you expected a Serb counterattack because you were, after all, motivated to save them, to help them as much as you could?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that we were not able to control thousands of refugees who were out looking for food. We didn't have anywhere to take them to, to protect them, to give them shelter. We didn't have any possibility to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I've heard at length your evidence about the hardships under which you -- you and the people with you -- lived in at that time. I'm not asking you about that, and I accept that. You're pushing on an open door if you think that I don't accept that. But what I'm interested in is this: You say that you were concerned about saving the lives of these civilians. You've conducted this action at Gornji Ratkovici and you expect -- you expect an imminent Serb counterattack such that you leave the area and quickly go and take up your positions. That must of necessity left these civilians, these helpless civilians, according to your evidence, exposed to there Serb counterattack, whatever form it might take, infantry attacks or bombing. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we returned quickly in order to prevent an infantry breakthrough, if there was such an attack by the Serbs in our area, but of course we couldn't get the civilians back to return so quickly. Of course we wanted to have them return and we told them they shouldn't go in the first place. But at that point in time, it wasn't possible to control the situation because a person who didn't have anything to eat and who went out looking for food, you couldn't do much. The option they were facing was to die in one way or another. That was the reason why people had to go. If they didn't go, they would die of hunger, and if they did go and were not killed during the excursion, then they would be able to bring back something to eat so there would be the possibility that they would then survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb civilians who stayed in the area of Ratkovici were able to stay for quite a while in the area, scouring the area and seeing what they could collect. Would you -- do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the Serb civilians. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Muslim civilians. MR. DI FAZIO: I've got -- I'm grateful to you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope you understood what I meant. I apologise. I'm talking about the Muslim, Bosniak civilians. They were able to stay in the area and scour the area for materials and so on?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They stayed to scour the area, to look for food, and, much later, they would go also to look for food and then they would return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said in your evidence yesterday that after the attack, you noticed them coming back to your village, to the village - to the village, I don't know which village, but the village - carrying building materials, windows, doors and food. Now, I suggest to you that in order for them to be able to get --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I suggest to you that in order for them to get this material, that sort of material, windows, doors and so on, required some dismantling and that they must have been able to stay in the area to secure these materials for some time, quite some time. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say that they were there for some time but I don't know. Your Honour, what does the Prosecutor mean when he says that time is required? You don't really need a lot of time to take a window, or dismantle a window from a house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. I'll be clearer. Let me ask you this: When did the Serb bombardment start which caused death of all those -- of those civilians in the area of Ratkovici? What time did it start on the 21st of June? This is the expected counterattack.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question so that I can understand it better?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. I'm still talking to you about this episode that -- in Ratkovici and Gornji Ratkovici and the area on the 21st of June. You already told us how you left immediately to go and take up your positions for the expected counterattack and you've testified that, yes, there was a counterattack, yes it was artillery, and that a number of Muslim civilians were killed. What time did this artillery counterattack occur, what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the counterattack?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Serb bombing.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That took place in the afternoon. I don't know the exact time or the hour, but it was after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, afternoon, after 12.00. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please. May I suggest a somewhat shorter break? I can then consolidate and also hopefully leave the time for some re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am noticing the witness is getting tired. That's number one. It is quite evident actually, visually evident. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have been sitting for an hour and a half. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had the previous break because of the technical problems that we had extended from half an hour -- 25 minutes to exactly one hour. So I don't know how much more you have left, how much time you require. MR. DI FAZIO: I will finish today, easily. I would hope that I would have no more than about 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I would suggest is -- MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Half and hour. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: I better say half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's play it safe because I suppose there might be re-examination on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You require how much time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think about 15 minutes, 20 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we -- yeah, but I was going to suggest that we try not to stay beyond the time that we have allocated. Could I ask everyone to agree that we will have a ten-minute break only for the time being? MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's fine with you but I want to know if it's fine with everyone who are working with us, the technicians, interpreters, and then we should be able to finish at quarter to 2.00, 1.45.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay, let's break and restart sharp in ten-minutes' time. In the meantime, make sure the witness is given a coffee or something, that he's given an opportunity to rest a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally before you continue, I mean just to inform you, I hope you agree with this, but you know that when we had the technical problem and we happened to be in private session, we were discussing that matter informally at the time because we were going to raise it properly later on. I've been asked whether we want it in the transcript, incorporated. I think we can leave it and we will deal with it again tomorrow, all right? MR. DI FAZIO: That suits the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please and Mr. Ramic as well, I've really got one topic left and I won't take up the whole half hour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better. MR. DI FAZIO: -- I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better. I hope Madam Vidovic will copy you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a fellow called Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that you've never met him, you're not an acquaintance or friend of his, not now and not back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never met him, then or now. And he doesn't know me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. What about a gentleman named Akif Ustic? Have you ever -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him because he was a teacher, but we didn't really know each other personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that -- did he die in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question so that I know exactly who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. Did -- Akif Ustic, was he killed in Fakovici on or around -- on the 5th of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so, actually. What -- anyway, that's -- he's giving evidence. He was killed but -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sorry, to clarify that: Are you saying that you don't know in Akif Ustic was killed in Fakovici or you don't know he was killed. I assume you do know he died, he was killed during the war.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed but I don't know where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, you know where Suceska is, don't you, a place called Suceska?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of it but I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that it's to the west of Srebrenica, quite some distance from the villages that you've been -- that you described today and yesterday, down Poznanovici and those places? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know how far it is from our villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's certainly -- I mean I'm looking at a map here. I don't want to mislead you. It's clearly further away from you than Srebrenica is. You'd have to agree with that, wouldn't you? And if you --

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's twice the distance, if Srebrenica is 20 kilometres away then Suceska is another 20 kilometres, a total of 40 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I remind you of your evidence that -- yesterday that you couldn't even communicate with other villages in your area. Do you recall that evidence? At least some of them, not all of them, but some of them you couldn't even communicate with, the Muslim villages, I mean.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember saying that I couldn't communicate, and I know exactly which period I was referring to. I mentioned it. It was up until sometime in the summer. I think that's what it says there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And furthermore, communication was non-existent, you say, don't you, with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the March, April, May, June period, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday in your evidence you also touched upon an event that occurred at Fakovici some days later -- or some time later, in 1992. Do you remember talking about that? And you said that you'd actually -- you were there, you went there on -- in fact you had the date on this, I recall, incorrectly. You had the 5th of October but you didn't actually go into Fakovici itself on that date. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you fighting at Fakovici on that day, on the 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said exactly where I went. I wasn't in Fakovici, not in Fakovici itself. I was in Gornji Fakovici, a distance away, and from there, you can see with the naked eye, and of course with the binoculars, you can see Fakovici. I know Fakovici very well because I went to school there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see Mr. Akif Ustic on that -- well, I withdraw that question. I think I'm safe in saying, aren't I, that you didn't see Zulfo Tursunovic or Akif Ustic in Fakovici on that day; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have been surprised to have seen fighters or men from Suceska in Fakovici on the 5th of October 1992, engaged in fighting against Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I never went to Suceska and that I knew very few people from there. I didn't know Zulfo, and even if somebody was there, it would be safe to assume that it was because of food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your evidence is that communications between these small villages, Muslim-held -- Muslim villages in your area was extremely problematical or non-existent, and as far as communication with places further away, such as Srebrenica, impossible. So would you agree that, if what you say is correct, it would not have been possible or feasible for fighters to go from a place called Suceska to Fakovici on the 5th of October? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness answered very clearly that the non-existence or difficulty with communication with those Muslim villages was up to June 1992, that's what his answer was directed to. And so obviously it shouldn't be suggested that he gave that answer in relation to October 1992. He was very clear about the period he was referring to and the places he was referring to. So as long as those two aren't run together then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a very valid objection and you either rephrase your question to inquire what the position -- whether the position remained the same after June or whether it changed. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm very grateful to Mr. Jones and he's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is, definitely. Incidentally, Akif Ustic, I checked, he died in Zaluzje when he tried to take -- and that was June, Zaluzje or something like that. But forget it. It's certainly not Fakovici in October. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- was the situation as regards communication between the Muslim-held villages in your area and communication with Srebrenica different following June of 1992? In other words, did it improve?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that after June, at some point in July, there was a certain amount of improvement in terms of communications but I said earlier on the communication between Suceska, Srebrenica, Poznanovici, that is to say Fakovici, we are talking about more than 40 kilometres so I leave it up to you to judge what kind of communication could have taken place there, and how long it would take for any news to get to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, if you don't know, just please tell us, but don't leave it up to me to judge because you're in a far better position than I was -- I am. Are you aware of any improvement in communication facilities as between the Muslim villages in your area and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the course of the month of July, that is to say much, much later, it was possible to have some kind of communication, at a certain point, but as to whether anyone was actually able to get to Fakovici from Suceska, I don't believe so, because it was just too far. Your Honour, in those times, there were no vehicles available. You had to travel on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's interesting evidence that you tell us of. If Your Honours please, I want to show a clip from the interview with Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: And I -- unfortunately I think I need to know the Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either 318 or 319. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour has it at your fingertips. That's for the purposes of the transcript. Perhaps while the case manager investigates that I'll continue and, on the other hand, I need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's either 318 or 319 or both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 348 and 349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 348 and 349, or 328 or 329. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm told it's P329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 328 and 329. Okay. P329. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know which one this clip is from. I'll look into it and -- sorry, I can now be clear. This clip is from Exhibit P329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 329. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Ramic, I want to show you very brief, very brief indeed, and as you look at it you'll understand it, okay? MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours can follow the transcript at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's correct. MR. DI FAZIO: If it's correct, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "I told that Sefik Mandic died that day. The commander of the [unintelligible] TO. That's what I do know. "Were there any other soldiers of this Territorial Defence during the advance of [unintelligible]. "And I also know that some of his soldiers were killed by a cannon when the shelling started. When they were collecting food, a couple of them were killed there. "Zulfo's men were the ones that took the village of Fakovici? "Yeah. Zulfo's and Akif's and the Territorial Defences of Biljeg and [unintelligible]. The biggest stronghold was by this camp. The main fighting that there was, was here." MR. DI FAZIO: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Oric was there talking about a gentleman named Zulfo taking -- being involved in an action at Fakovici. Bearing in mind what you've just seen of the clip, bearing in mind everything that you know of events in 1992, and bearing in mind your knowledge of the geography in the area of 1992, would you agree that a man such as Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic could make it from an area of Suceska with fighters to go and fight in Fakovici in October of 1992? That's all I'm asking you. I'm not asking you if it happened, if it's true. I'm just asking you: Could he have managed that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have interpretation or could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, can I ask you to repeat your answer, please? You said [B/C/S spoken] something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He could not. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Mr. Ramic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Do you need sometime for consultation? Yes. Yes, Madam Vidovic, re-examination. Re-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I'm going to make sure I'm as brief as possible. Good day to you again. Have I understood you correctly in that you said today that you heard about Mr. Oric only as late as after the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in the period of time prior to the demilitarisation and prior to the fall of your village, Poznanovici and the surrounding small villages, Dedici, Podkorjen, and Kakarici [phoen], did you ever hear from anyone who was familiar with the situation there that Oric was leading the attack at Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that and I had never seen Mr. Oric, and I myself was there on the spot. I would have seen him, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we just go back to this book for a moment, the book that my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you about? A part of the book by Nijaz Masic. First of all did you ever meet Mr. Nijaz Masic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not as such, not in person. I knew of him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of the fact that Mr. Nijaz Masic, after the fall of Srebrenica, fell ill and that he spent a long time in treatment due to psychiatric problems?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask, Your Honours, if you don't mind, to show the witness the excerpt from this book Srebrenica, and I would like to ask you, sir -- I can't remember the Exhibit number now I do apologise, but at any rate, Mr. Ramic, I'd like you to take a look at the preface and could you look at the list of people, the list of names, indicated as people providing source materials for the book written by Mr. Masic? Could you look at the first page which it says "Srebrenica: The Aggression, the Resistance, Treason, Genocide," et cetera, and you've got the date when the book was published, July 1999. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it. I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the cover page before the introduction. It's the title of the book, Srebrenica, and can you see that it says July 1999?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we go back to the introduction now where we've got the long list of people who provided source materials for the book, and could you just run through the list, and yesterday we talked about Vekaz Husic, for example. Can you read this list carefully? Did -- I mean, these people, such as, for example, Vekaz Husic, did they ever get out of Srebrenica alive, and after the events of 1995, would have -- would they have been in a position to talk to Mr. Masic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think so because quite a few of them are not alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In this respect, let me ask you the following question. Have you ever heard of Mr. Masic having ever been in touch with Mr. Malkic? Yesterday you said that you are close to Mr. Dzevad Malkic. Have you ever heard of him talking about list war-time experiences to Mr. Masic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Naser Oric or anyone else on this list for that matter ever talked about their experiences to Mr. Masic?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just go back to this bit that we referred to earlier on with regard to the translation, the liquidation of Chetnik strongholds. Could you just tell us once again in our own language does "liquidation" mean the same thing as "destruction"?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And another point now. The reference is made here to Osmace, Kragljivoda, Stari Grad fighters, and so on. In the period of time of June 1992, or on that day, on the 21st of June 1992, did you get in touch with fighters from those units, Kragljivoda, Osata [phoen], et cetera, at all?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not because I said that there was no possibility to get in touch with anyone. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. When you talked about the event that took place on the 8th of June 1992, the Prosecutor asked you whether the refugees were able to see the Serbs and then run off into the woods. In relation to this I'm going to put the following question to you: Do you remember that you told us in some detail yesterday, and you mentioned it today, that is to say the killing of two Muslims on their way to Podkorjen?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: Did the refugees -- I mean was this mass of people able to hear the shots, the -- fired on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was nearby. Everybody could hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let me ask you something in relation to the 21st of June. You said that you saw masses of people behind you when you turned to look. You said that yesterday and you said it again today in reply to a question put to you by the Prosecutor. Do you remember whether you saw anyone that you would be able to describe as a soldier in this mass of refugees?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on that occasion, looking at that mass of people, see anything that you could describe as a military unit, something that would be described as a military unit from some of the other villages, not from your area?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did say they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much and let me just dwell on the matter of Mr. Dzevad Malkic for a moment. The Prosecutor asked whether Mr. Dzevad Malkic issued orders or instructions to you to the effect that no property should be destroyed. He also asked whether it was a usual phenomenon at the time. And my question is this: Prior to these events, on the 21st of June 1992, that is, had you ever heard or seen anything about any destruction of any Serb property in your surroundings?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to these instructions and orders, in June 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. MR. DI FAZIO: That was just an accidental nudging of a button here. It certainly wasn't intended to sabotage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I didn't realise what was happening and I think no one did except, of course, Mr. Di Fazio. So can I ask you, Madam Vidovic, to repeat your question please, and my apologies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Di Fazio is trying to confuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's just a joke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I've mentioned that the Prosecutor asked you about these instructions and orders issued by Mr. Mandic in this period - Malkic, sorry, I do apologies - in this period of time, June 1992, and in this respect, I'm going to ask you the following question: In May and June 1992, did Mr. Malkic issue any orders or instructions? Was he in a position to issue any orders or instructions in such a situation? Could you explain that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not in a position to issue any orders because quite simply as I mentioned, this was a group of volunteers and nobody at the time was in a position to order anything. People were volunteers so there was no possibility to issue any orders, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And something else now. Mr. Ramic, as to these talks about the torching of Serb property and so on, are you able to answer this question? Do you know anything about it? Was it a matter of him simply explaining his opinion as to how the Muslims should act, if they should behave in the same way as Serbs or not? What was the matter there?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that he simply made these statements and he said to us what he thought and some of us embraced that attitude. But there were no orders there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Ramic, let me put this to you in this way: The fact that he made those statements or talked about his views on the torching, did he do it because he knew of anything like that having taken place or was he simply giving you advice as to what you should do with regard to other people's property?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He simply was of the view that we should not be doing that, that we were not the same as Serbs, and he was simply a wise man, a good man, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You were asked a whole series of questions here about whether it was possible or not, and that at a later stage in October 1992, whether it was possible or not to get from Suceska to Fakovici. Do you know whether Tursunovic was there or not?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know in what way Oric would have received that information in case he had received it at all? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that's neither a clarification of anything that I raised in evidence and from all the evidence this witness has given he would be the last person who could tell you that. He didn't even meet Mr. Oric. He's never met Mr. Oric, and he's given you evidence about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the objection has to be sustained. You need to rephrase your question and perhaps you can ask the witness to explain how Mr. Oric, according to that interview, would have given that particular description of events, if he can enlighten us on it, because if obviously he cannot, then he will not give us any information, if you want to persist in the question, of course, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any idea as to what Mr. Oric could and could not have known?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps somebody could have reported some information, some stories, to him. He could have received some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do not know that?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, do you have -- yes, my colleague, Judge Brydensholt, has got a question for you. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going back to the 8th of June, Metaljka, the fight there. Could you describe for me the Serbs who arrived there, did they approach your village through a road and how was that road? Could they have spread out if they so wanted? And how many do you believe they were?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit of a comprehensive question. Could you just repeat it once again, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. What way did the Serb soldiers come? Was it on a road or was it in a free area, on a field or something?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not really a road. It's a forest path, a forest path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Would it have been possible for them to spread out or should they stay, because there was only this path, together?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since probably I was not able to see all of them, I suppose that some individuals may have been scattered all over the area because, at a later stage, when we searched the area, I did see that there were those machine-guns in several places in the forest and we could see that they were cutting down some trees which were in their way. So I don't think they were all in one place. They must have been scattered around the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And could you tell us how many on your side were? How many fighters in your group?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten, ten, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And then on the 21st of June, when the Serb soldiers approached you in the wood, how did they do that? Did they come along a road or over fields or how did you see them?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the fields. Across the fields, and along the road as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And how would you describe the route the civilians behind you took when they came out of the wood? Would they be in a group or would they be in a long line or over several fields, or how would they look?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes, the refugees and your own civilians.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, the civilians were just going in as they best could, as they felt would be best or safest. Some went in groups. Some went across the fields. Others through the woods, and others along the road. It was not really organised or controlled. They all made their own decisions as to what to do, whether they were going to follow a group of people or just to move on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But could you describe to us, if you looked back and saw them, would you see a line of several hundred metres of a massive group of people or would it be more in a column, in that way disciplined group that they followed each other. Or would they be spread around?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of columns spread around all over the place. There were a number of separate columns without any sort of formal organisation. They were just on their way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And the last question: How many Serb soldiers do you think were on their way approaching you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a bit difficult to answer that because certainly I wasn't in a position to see all Serb soldiers, but roughly 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've got two very short questions. And the second one very much depends on what the answer to the first one will be. You will recall, Mr. Ramic, that you were asked questions about that alleged meeting in Bajramovici in May of 1992, and you said that you did not attend it, no one from your group attended and you would have -- basically, you would have been informed. Who would have informed you of the holding of such a meeting or similar meetings? Who would have informed you?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that if anyone had known, Dzevad Malkic would have known because we considered him to be a kind of leader, and that's what I meant, that he would have known, and that's why I said that nobody attended and we didn't know about a meeting like that. So I had him in mind. In case he had attended he would have at least told us so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how would he have been approached and by whom, to inform him of such a meeting or similar meetings?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said -- I mean, your question was whether I knew about that meeting, and if he was at the meeting, he had no need for anyone to tell him about it. He would have known. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other meetings that took place around about the same time?

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, no. I said that we were an enclave that was under siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely why I'm asking you, because you said you would have been informed about it. How would it have been possible to inform you or Mr. Malkic about such a meeting or similar meetings roundabout the same time, if you were so cut off from the rest of the -- let him answer the question first, please, Madam.

utterances.speaker: OMER RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't possible. There was no way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay. Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now it's all right but I would like to ask you, the witness was actually saying that there was no way at any point in time of the witness mentioning anybody who would tell them from outside Srebrenica. However, the witness said that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely why I asked him the question because if we had left it where he had left it, namely I would have known about it, it meant that there was a possibility of coming to know about it, Madam Vidovic. So that brings your testimony to an end, Mr. Ramic. And we've done our utmost to make it possible for you to return home by tomorrow. On behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of the Trial Chamber of my colleague, Judge Brydensholt, my colleague, Judge Eser, who couldn't be with us, and also on my own behalf, I thank you for coming over to give testimony. You will receive all the attention and assistance you require now to facilitate your travel back home at the earliest possible opportunity, and on behalf of everyone present here I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also wish to take this opportunity to acknowledge publicly the cooperation of everyone today, like on many other previous occasions, to make this possible. Because had I encountered resistance, this witness wouldn't have finished his testimony today. So I thank the technicians, the interpreters, Defence plus Prosecution, and our staff for having cooperated. Thank you.
